summary: A list of well-known socket numbers that Jon Postel assigned for public functions on the early ARPANET, with a general scheme for ranges such as network-wide standard functions and experimental ones. Sockets here were the addressing scheme of the old network control program, before ports. It was replaced by RFC 503.

eli5.summary: A phone book of special numbers that early network computers agreed to use for particular services, like a list of which door leads to which service.

subtitle: Well-known socket numbers that early ARPANET computers agreed to use for standard services.

tldr.problem: Early ARPANET computers needed to know which numbered sockets to use for common services like Telnet, file transfer, and email, so clients could connect to the right service.
tldr.mechanism: Jon Postel established a numbering scheme: sockets 0-63 for network-wide standard functions, 64-127 for host-specific functions, 128-239 reserved, and 240-255 for experiments. The RFC assigns numbers to specific services like Telnet (socket 1), File Transfer (3), and Echo (7).
tldr.outcome: This scheme became the standard for addressing services on the early ARPANET, though it was later replaced by the more flexible port concept in TCP/IP.

today: RFC 433 is a historic document superseded by RFC 503. It established the socket numbering scheme that became foundational to ARPANET addressing.

sections.title: Socket Number Assignments
sections.content:
RFC 433 publishes the standard assignments for socket numbers used for public functions on the early ARPANET. Jon Postel, designated the czar of socket numbers, established a 40-bit addressing scheme where the first 8 bits identified the host, the next 24 bits were site-specific, and the final 8 bits (called the AEN, Another Eightbit Number) identified the specific service.

The RFC defines ranges for different categories of services and assigns numbers to well-known functions that all ARPANET sites could use.
sections.eli5: A socket number is like a room number in a big office building. The first digits say which building, the last digits say what service is there.

sections.title: Socket Number Ranges
sections.content:
The numbering scheme divides socket space into regions: sockets 0-63 are Network Wide Standard Functions available on all hosts, sockets 64-127 are Host Specific Functions, sockets 128-239 are reserved for future use, and sockets 240-255 are open for experimental functions.

Well-known services include Telnet (1), File Transfer (3), Remote Job Entry (5), Echo (7), Discard (9), and Character Generator (19). Some sockets like 241 (NCP Measurement) and 243 (Survey Measurement) serve network operations.
sections.eli5: Low numbers like 1, 3, and 7 are for everyone to use. Higher numbers are for experiments or special sites.

sections.title: Deployed Services
sections.content:
The RFC also lists actual services running on various ARPANET hosts using these sockets. UCLA-NMC offers Telnet (1) and measurement sockets (241, 243). SRI-ARC offers Telnet (1), File Transfer (3), Echo (5), CPYNET (7), and SYSTAT (9). BBN-TENEX and other major sites offer Telnet, File Transfer, and various network utilities on assigned sockets.

The RFC notes that some hosts run services on non-standard socket numbers and requests operators to report any missing or incorrect entries.
sections.eli5: Different computers on the network offer different services on these numbered sockets, and the RFC lists which ones actually work.

sections.title: Status Today
sections.content: This RFC was replaced by RFC 503. The socket numbering scheme later evolved into the port concept in TCP/IP, which is still used today in modern networks.
sections.eli5: This system of assigning service numbers got updated later, and the basic idea became how modern networks work.

references.text: Postel, J. and N. Neigus, "Socket Number List", RFC 503, December 1972.
